title: Two Voices, One Page
bigQuestion: Why do people study the Talmud with a partner, out loud, instead of alone and quiet?

story.title: Stuck on the Same Word
story.kicker: Two kids share one big page, and one word stops them both.
paragraphs: Maya and Leo sit at one desk. One big book is open between them. It is a page of the Talmud. The words are small. Some are Hebrew. Some are Aramaic, an old language. Their teacher says, "Read it together. Out loud."

Maya reads a line. Leo reads the next line. Then they both stop. There is a word they do not know. Maya says, "I think it means a lamp." Leo says, "I think it means a door." They look at each other. They are stuck on the same word.
Maya does not get mad. She says, "Show me why you think door." Leo points to the line above. It talks about a house. Maya nods. Then she points to the line below. It talks about light. Leo nods too.

Their teacher walks by. "Good," she says. "That is how the rabbis did it. Two people. One page. Lots of questions." Maya and Leo laugh. They still do not know the word. But they know more than they did.
story.think: Maya and Leo did not agree. What did they do instead of fighting? Why did that help?

lessons.title: What a Chavruta Is
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud in pairs, out loud, with questions.
reading: The Talmud is not read alone in a quiet corner. It is studied with a partner. The word for a study partner is *chavruta*. It comes from a word that means friend.
Two partners sit at one page. One reads. The other listens. Then they trade. They ask each other, "What does this mean?" They talk out loud. The room gets noisy.
A room for this kind of study has a name. It is a beit midrash. That means house of study. Jews have studied this way for a very long time.

words.d: a study partner; two people who read the Talmud together and ask each other questions
a house of study, a room where people learn Talmud, often in pairs and out loud

look.title: Picture the Room
look.text: Look at a long room with long tables. At every table, two people sit close. One big book is open between them. One person points at a line. The other shakes her head and points at a different line. Everyone is talking. Nobody is shouting. It is loud, but it is happy.
look.prompt: What do you see the partners doing? Why do you think they sit two by two?

check.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

check.q: How do partners study the Talmud?
check.why: Partners read out loud and ask each other questions. The room is noisy.
Beit midrash means house of study. People learn there, often in pairs.

lessons.title: Get Yourself a Friend
lessons.mainIdea: Pirkei Avot says: find a teacher, and get yourself a friend to study with.
reading: There is a small book inside the Mishnah. It is called *Pirkei Avot*. That means chapters of the fathers. It is full of short sayings by rabbis.
One saying comes from a rabbi named Joshua ben Perachyah. He lived about 2,100 years ago. He said: get yourself a teacher. And get yourself a friend to learn with.
Jewish tradition reads this as a rule for study. A teacher shows you the way. A friend walks it with you. That friend is your chavruta.

words.d: a short book of rabbis' sayings inside the Mishnah; the name means chapters of the fathers

look.title: A Saying to Remember
look.text: Joshua ben Perachyah said: Make yourself a teacher, get yourself a friend to study with, and judge every person on the good side.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:6, retold in simple words; compare Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: The saying has three parts. Say them in your own words. Which one is about a chavruta?

check.why: Pirkei Avot means chapters of the fathers. It is a book of sayings.

check.q: What did Joshua ben Perachyah say to get?
check.why: His saying tells a learner to find a teacher and a friend to study with.
Pirkei Avot is a short book inside the Mishnah.

lessons.title: Two Houses That Argued
lessons.mainIdea: The students of Hillel and Shammai disagreed a lot, and still stayed friends.
reading: Hillel and Shammai were two rabbis. They lived about 2,000 years ago. Their students kept arguing after them. The Talmud calls the students two houses. The House of Hillel and the House of Shammai.
The two houses disagreed about many rules. They argued about food, holidays and weddings. The Talmud says they argued about some rules for three years.
But the Mishnah tells us something else. The two houses still married each other's children. They argued hard. They stayed one people. Jewish tradition remembers that.

words.d: the students who followed Hillel's way of reading the rules
the students who followed Shammai's way of reading the rules

look.title: Still One Family
look.text: The Mishnah says the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel disagreed about some marriage rules. Even so, the men of one house married women from the other house.
look.cite: Mishnah Yevamot 1:4, retold in simple words
look.prompt: The two houses disagreed. What does marrying each other's children show about them?

check.q: Who were the House of Hillel?
check.why: The House of Hillel means the students who followed Hillel's way.

check.q: What did the two houses still do?
check.why: The Mishnah says the two houses still married each other's children.

check.q: How long did the Talmud say one argument lasted?
check.why: The Talmud says the houses argued about some rules for three years.

lessons.title: Both Sides Can Be Right
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says both houses spoke words of the living God, and the rule follows Hillel.
reading: The Talmud tells a story about the long argument. After three years, a voice came from heaven. The voice spoke about both houses. It said: these and those are words of the living God.
Then the voice said the rule follows the House of Hillel. Why? The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle. They taught Shammai's side first. Then they taught their own.
Jewish tradition reads this story in many ways. One reading is simple. You can lose an argument and still have said something true. And being kind helps you win.

words.d: what the Talmud's story calls both sides of the argument between the two houses

look.title: The Long Argument
rows: Sides called words of the living God
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b, retold in simple words
look.prompt: Two sides were called true. Only one side became the rule. How can both things be so?

check.q: What did the voice call both sides?
check.why: The Talmud's story says these and those are words of the living God.

check.q: Why does the Talmud say the rule follows Hillel?
choices: His students were gentle and taught the other side first
check.why: The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and taught Shammai's view before their own.

check.q: In which tractate is this story found?
check.why: The story of the voice and the two houses is in Eruvin 13b.

sections.title: How to Be a Good Partner

lessons.title: Ask When You Are Stuck
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel said a shy person cannot learn, so a good partner asks questions.
reading: Pirkei Avot has a saying from Hillel. He said: a shy person cannot learn. And a person with a hot temper cannot teach.
What does that mean? If you are too shy to ask, you stay stuck. If you get angry fast, no one wants to ask you. So a good chavruta asks. And a good chavruta stays calm.
The rabbis liked questions. Another rabbi, Chanina, said he learned a lot from his teachers. He learned more from his friends. He learned the most from his students. Their questions taught him.

words.d: what you ask when you do not understand; the rabbis said questions are how you learn

look.title: Two Things Hillel Said
look.text: Hillel said: A shy person does not learn, and a person who gets angry easily does not teach.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 2:5, retold in simple words; compare Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Why would being shy stop you from learning? What could a partner do to help?

check.q: Who cannot learn, in Hillel's saying?
check.why: Hillel said a shy person cannot learn, because that person does not ask.

check.q: Who did Rabbi Chanina say he learned the most from?
check.why: Rabbi Chanina said he learned most from his students and their questions (Ta'anit 7a).

check.q: What should you do when you are stuck?
check.why: A good chavruta asks. The rabbis said questions are how you learn.

lessons.title: Say Why, Gently
lessons.mainIdea: A study partner is a friend who makes you think, so you say why, not just no.
reading: Sometimes your partner is wrong. What do you do? You do not just say no. You say why. You point to the page. You show the line. And you say it gently.
The Talmud tells of two partners. They were Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. One taught a rule. The other asked many hard questions. The Talmud says that made the rule clear.
Later, Rabbi Yochanan lost his partner. Someone else came to study with him. That person only agreed. Rabbi Yochanan was sad. He missed the hard questions. A friend who makes you think is a gift.

words.d: in a soft, kind way; how a good partner says you are wrong
a rabbi in the Talmud whose hard questions helped his partner Rabbi Yochanan think

look.title: Two Ways to Say It
look.text: Partner A says: "No. You are wrong. That is dumb." Partner B says: "Hmm. I read it a different way. Look at this line. It says the lamp is by the door. Does that change it?" Both partners think the same thing. Only one of them is a good chavruta.
look.prompt: Which partner would you want? Say what Partner B did that Partner A did not.

check.q: What do you do when your partner is wrong?
check.why: A good partner says why, points to the page, and stays gentle.

check.q: Who was Rabbi Yochanan's study partner?
check.why: Resh Lakish was Rabbi Yochanan's partner. His questions made the rules clear.

check.q: Why was Rabbi Yochanan sad with his new partner?
check.why: The Talmud says the new partner only agreed, and Rabbi Yochanan missed the hard questions.

review.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

review.q: How is the Talmud usually studied?
review.why: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud in pairs, out loud, with questions.

review.q: Which two houses argued for three years?
review.why: The Talmud says the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai argued for three years (Eruvin 13b).

review.q: What did the Mishnah say the two houses still did?
review.why: Mishnah Yevamot 1:4 says the houses still married each other's children.

review.q: Hillel said a shy person cannot do what?
review.why: Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot is that a shy person cannot learn.

review.q: What did Resh Lakish give his partner?
review.why: The Talmud says Resh Lakish asked many hard questions, and that made the rules clear.
